title: Your old men shall dream (Joel 2:28–29)
hookLine: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; Peter quoted it at Pentecost

lines: NINE IN THE MORNING, A FESTIVAL CROWD.
PETER STANDS UP AND QUOTES JOEL.
cards: Nine in the morning in Jerusalem, a festival crowd in the streets, and a commotion.

A small group of Jesus's followers pour out of a house, talking in languages they never learned, and visitors from many nations hear their own home tongues. Some are amazed; others laugh: they're drunk.
Then Peter, a fisherman who not long before had denied he even knew Jesus, stands up. It's too early in the day for that, he says.
And instead of explaining, he quotes an old prophet, from a book so short it's easy to flip past: Joel.

teach.b: Joel is only three or four chapters long, and nobody is sure exactly when he lived. His book opens with a disaster: locusts strip the land bare.
He calls the people to fast and turn back to God, and then the promises come, rain and harvest, then something bigger.

teach.h: SONS AND DAUGHTERS, OLD AND YOUNG.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions." Look at the list.
Sons and daughters, not just sons. Old and young.
Then further: "And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit." Servants.

In earlier stories of the Hebrew Bible, the spirit comes on particular people: a judge like Gideon, a king like Saul, a prophet. Joel pictures it soaked into everyone, like rain on a field after the locusts.
And old people dreaming means nobody has aged out of hearing from God. Now Acts chapter two.
Peter tells the crowd: "But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." Christians remember that day as Pentecost, and some call it the birthday of the church.

teach.h: YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS.
teach.b: Jews read Joel too, and hear his promise their own way, as a hope for Israel's renewal. For Christians, Peter's sermon made Joel's list the guest list of the church.

This week brought a field bought in wartime, dry bones, a heart of flesh, a furnace, a lions' den, a child learning to walk, and now the spirit on everyone. Over and over, the prophets refuse to give up on people.

how: Some churches read Joel 2:28–29 near Pentecost, alongside Acts 2, where Peter quotes it; churches that keep the Christian year celebrate Pentecost seven weeks after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit.

o: the day Jesus was baptized in the Jordan River
the day Jesus rose from the dead in Jerusalem
the day the spirit came and Peter quoted Joel

games.q: who's who on Joel's list — tap the pairs.
p: this is that, spoken by Joel

s: it names sons and daughters, and then servants and handmaids too.
Peter quoted Joel to explain Pentecost
"this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel," in Acts chapter two.
we know exactly when Joel lived
his book gives no date, and scholars still disagree about it.

games.q: you're Peter. a crowd hears your friends speaking in other languages, and some laugh that you're all drunk. what do you do?
o: slip away before it gets worse.
stand up and quote an old prophet.
argue about how much wine is too much.
games.why: he stands up, says it's far too early in the day to be drunk, and quotes Joel: "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel."

practice: Picture the oldest person you know and the youngest. Ask when you last listened to either without correcting, what the old one might still be dreaming, and what the young one might be seeing that you've stopped seeing.
If you pray, pray Joel's promise over them in its own words; if not, just hold them both for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Pentecost. The day Peter quoted Joel's promise that God's spirit would pour out on everyone, now remembered as the church's birthday.

orig.note: Hebrew: spirit, breath, wind. what Joel says God will pour out on all flesh.

carryVoice: Your line: on all flesh. Nobody ages out of hearing from God. Day four hundred eighty-three, and another week walked.
